title: Cap. VI: Maresius cited — friendship reply; consequent vs antecedent imputation
pass_a_gloss: At Groningen in 1646 Maresius published an elenctic theology synopsis answering Tirinus the Jesuit. In controversy 20 on the first parents and original sin, number 4, he digresses into imputing Adam's first disobedience, names Socinus, Curcellaeus, the French National Synod Decree, and Rivetus's booklet, then says not only the adversaries attack that imputation, but also — and this occasioned the Decree — his former sweet fellow-student Placeus of Saumur wholly rejects it beyond right and law while rightly defending hereditary corruption: both must stand, walking together, yet so that by nature's order the first sin's imputation precedes the transplant of inborn corruption. Placeus gladly recalls that student bond and owns the praises, though unworthy; he wishes Maresius writing against the Jesuit had left this supposed controversy alone, and hates being packed with Curcellaeus, from whom he sharply differs. He hopes Maresius will later affirm Placeus was not condemned by the National Synod and does not reject all imputation of Adam's first sin — God's glory and the church's building do not require treating him as condemned by everyone. If Maresius meant consequent imputation walking with corruption, Placeus would not resist; but he seems to mean antecedent, and to that Placeus cannot assent. Antecedent imputation does not clash with Scripture and reason; hereditary corruption is most surely proved by many Scriptures, many reasons, and experience itself. After this preface Maresius adds a few very short arguments, which Placeus will answer as briefly.
pass_b_english: There came forth at Groningen from John Nicolas in the year of the Lord 1646 A New Synopsis of Elenctic Theology, or Index of the controversies of the faith from the Holy Scriptures compiled by Jacob Tirinus the Jesuit, and enlarged, emended, and refuted with a perpetual Censure, by Samuel Maresius, Doctor of Sacred Theology and ordinary Professor of the same Faculty in the Provincial Academy of Groningen and Omland. In which, Controversy 20, on the state of the first parents and on original sin, number 4, on occasion of certain words of Tirinus, the most distinguished man digresses into that Controversy on the imputation of Adam's first disobedience, and when he had made mention of Socinus, Curcellaeus, and others who deny all imputation of that sin, and also of the Decree of the National Synod of the Churches of France, and of the booklet edited by the distinguished Rivetus, he added: Not only do the opponents attack that imputation, but also (which was the occasion of that Synodical Decree) the Reverend, most learned and most celebrated man, my former most sweet fellow-soldier in studies, D. Josué Placeus, Disputations of Saumur, part I, page 206 and following, entirely rejects it beyond right and law, while he studies well and orthodoxly to defend the hereditary corruption which is in all: since both that ought to be admitted, and this is to be acknowledged, as walking with equal step; yet so that by order of nature, and by the notable reason of the transplant of inborn corruption, the imputation of the first sin should precede.

That he was his fellow-soldier in studies Placeus remembers not without pleasure, and he recognizes the remains of old friendship in those praises with which he sees himself adorned by him though least worthy: yet he would have wished that the most distinguished man, writing against the Jesuit, had not mentioned this controversy, if he thinks there is any between us, and he would not want to be packed by a friend into the same bundle, as it were, with Curcellaeus, from whom he vehemently differs. Hereafter, as I hope, the most learned man will think he should affirm that Placeus was neither condemned by the National Synod, nor does he entirely reject the imputation of Adam's first sin. For I do not think he will judge that God's glory and the church's edification demand that he be held for condemned by all. But as to what he says, that imputation and corruption walk with equal step — if he understood consequent imputation, he would not have me resisting; but since he seems to understand antecedent, I cannot assent to him. For that imputation is in no way, neither by Scripture nor by reason, repugnant to Scripture and reason; but this corruption can most certainly be proved by many testimonies of Scripture, by many reasons, and even by experience itself.
Having prefaced such things, the most distinguished man subjoins these few arguments in very brief words, to which we shall also reply most briefly.
source_text:
Prodiit Groningae apud Ioan. Nicolaum Anno Domini M. DC. XLVI. Theologiae Elenchticae nova Synopsis, sive Index controversiarum fidei ex sacris Scripturis a Iacobo Tirino Iesuita concinnatus, et Censura perpetua auctus, emendatus, refutatus, per Samuelem Maresium S. Theol. D. eiusdemque Facultatis Professorem ordinarium in Academia Provinciali Groningae et Omlandiae. In quo, Controversia xx. de statu primorum parentum et de peccato originali, Num. 4, occasione quorundam Tirini verborum, digreditur vir clarissimus in Controversiam istam de imputatione primae Adami inobedientiae, ac cum Socini, Curcellaei, aliorumque omnem imputationem illius peccati negantium, nec-non Decreti Synodi Nationalis Ecclesiarum Galliae, libellique a Cl. Riveto editi meminisset, subjecit: Nec solum οἱ ἐναντίοι illam imputationem impugnant, sed etiam (quae fuit occasio illius Decreti Synodici) Rev. doctissimus ac celeberrimus vir, meus quondam Commilito in studiis suavissimus D. Iosue Placeus Disput. Salmur. parte I. p. 206. et seqq. illam omnino rejicit praeter ius et fas, dum bene et orthodoxe studet propugnare haereditariam, quae omnibus inest, corruptionem: cum et illa debeat admitti, et haec sit agnoscenda, utpote quae pari passu ambulent; sic tamen ut ordine naturae, et insigni rationis traducem innatae corruptionis, primi peccati praecedat imputatio.

Ejus se Commilitonem in studiis non sine voluptate Placeus reminiscitur, veterisque amicitiae reliquias in elogiis illis agnoscit, quibus se minime dignum ab eo ornari videt: optasset tamen clarissimum virum adversus Iesuitam scribentem, hujus, si quam inter nos esse putat, controversiae non meminisse, nolletque se ab amico in eundem quasi fasciculum cum Curcellaeo, a quo vehementer dissentit, compactum esse. In posterum, uti spero, vir doctissimus Placeum neque condemnatum a Synodo Nationali fuisse, neque imputationem primi Adae peccati omnino rejicere, sibi affirmandum putabit. Non enim opinor, existimabit, Dei gloriam Ecclesiaeque aedificationem flagitare, ut pro condemnato ab omnibus habeatur. Quod autem ait, imputationem et corruptionem pari passu ambulare, si imputationem intelligeret consequentem, non me haberet repugnantem, sed cum antecedentem intelligere videatur, ei assentiri non possum. Illa enim imputatio nullo modo, nec Scriptura, nec ratione, Scripturae et rationi repugnans; haec vero corruptio multis Scripturae testimoniis, multis rationibus, ipsaque adeo experientia certissime probari potest.

Talia praefatus vir Clariss. subiungit haec pauca argumenta verbis brevissimis, quibus etiam brevissime respondebimus.
